SDK 1.0.0 · Bridge protocol v1
GitHub · Issues

Guide

Recipes

The nine things almost every integration ends up needing, each written out in full: the two form planes, reopening an application, what to do after a submission, answering an expired session, authenticated downloads, runtime locale and theme, a close button that does not throw away a half-filled form, and handing the form's HTTP to your own app.

React Native comes first in every recipe — it is the most-used path — and the other hosts appear where they genuinely differ. Several of these exist because the wrong version of them fails silently: a submission that lands against nobody, a download that quietly returns a login page, an approval queue that never advances. Where that is the case, the recipe says what the silent failure looks like.

An anonymous (public) form

Use this when the form must be fillable by someone who has not signed in — a public service request, a complaint, a careers application. Two things decide it and both fail quietly if you get them wrong: the request type must be anything other than the literal 'internal' (by convention 'external'), and init must carry no credential. In React Native that means omitting the auth prop entirely. The absence of the key is what tells the portal to use the public plane, and it is also what makes the portal drop credentials a previous signed-in launch left in the WebView's storage — without it, a stale token is attached to /Portal/PublicForms/* and every request comes back 401. 

<AmthalPortalForm
  config={{ baseUrl: PORTAL_BASE_URL }}
  /* no `auth` prop at all — not an empty object, not { token: '' } */
  request={{ kind: 'newApplication', type: 'external', productID: 830 }}
  onSubmitted={showReceipt}
  onCancelled={close}
  onCloseRequested={close}
  onError={showError}
/>

The native hosts declare it the opposite way

On iOS, Android and the Expo sheet the auth argument is not optional, so there is no key to omit. There, an empty token string is the anonymous declaration, and the portal treats a blank token as no credential: 

// Expo sheet
presentPortalSheet({
  config: { baseUrl: PORTAL_BASE_URL },
  auth: { token: '' },
  request: { kind: 'newApplication', type: 'external', productID: 830 },
  onSubmitted: (result) => showReceipt(result),
});
// iOS
AmthalPortalViewController.present(
    from: self,
    config: config,
    request: .newApplication(type: "external", productID: 830),
    auth: PortalAuth(token: ""),
    delegate: self
)

// Android
PortalFormActivity.start(
    context,
    config,
    PortalRequest.NewApplication(type = "external", productID = 830),
    PortalAuth(token = ""),
    listener,
)

Reach for { token: '' } only on those three. In React Native it is the shape the documentation tells you never to send — omit the prop instead.

A signed-in form

Use this when the submission must belong to the customer and show up in their own requests list. The whole difference is the request type: the portal tests type === "internal" and falls through for every other value. Open a signed-in user with 'external' and the form submits successfully, returns a reference number, and is filed against an anonymous stand-in — the customer never sees it again, and nothing anywhere reports an error. Pass the literal string. 

<AmthalPortalForm
  config={{ baseUrl: PORTAL_BASE_URL, locale: 'en' }}
  auth={{ token: session.token, branchId: '12', user: session.profile }}
  request={{ kind: 'newApplication', type: 'internal', productID: 830 }}
  onSubmitted={showReceipt}
  onCancelled={close}
  onCloseRequested={close}
  onError={showError}
/>

branchId is the tenant the forms and branding belong to, passed as a string. The third field, user, is optional: hand over the profile object your app already holds and the portal skips a profile round-trip; omit it and the portal rebuilds the user from the token.

The same session on the native hosts

The user object is the one field whose shape changes across platforms — it is a JSON string on both native hosts, under a name that differs by one letter's casing: 

// iOS  — userJSON
let auth = PortalAuth(token: token, branchId: "12", userJSON: profileJSONString)

// Android — userJson
val auth = PortalAuth(token = token, branchId = "12", userJson = profileJsonString)

Invalid JSON in that string is not an error: both hosts drop the user key and let the portal reconstruct the profile itself, so a malformed payload costs you a round-trip rather than a session. Android's PortalAuth.toString() redacts all three fields, so the object is safe to include in a log line — the values inside it never are.

Reopening an existing application

Every application the customer submits should be reachable again — to read back, to print, or to amend while it is still open. The two ids that make that possible arrive once, in FormSubmitResult, and are never re-derivable from the reference number: keep batchID and headerID when the submission lands, or read them off your own list screen. Without them the only route back into an application is starting a new one. 

<AmthalPortalForm
  config={{ baseUrl: PORTAL_BASE_URL }}
  auth={auth}
  request={{
    kind: 'existingApplication',
    type: 'internal',
    productID: 830,
    batchID: application.batchID,
    headerID: application.headerID,
    readOnly: true,          // false lets the customer amend it
  }}
  onSubmitted={close}
  onCancelled={close}
  onCloseRequested={close}
  onError={showError}
/>

type still selects the plane, exactly as it does for a new application — reopen a customer's own application with 'internal'.

Native takes strings where React Native takes either

FormSubmitResult.batchID and .headerID are typed number | string | undefined, and the React Native request accepts either. The Swift and Kotlin requests take String, so convert at the boundary rather than storing whichever type the portal happened to send: 

// iOS
request: .existingApplication(
    type: "internal", productID: 830,
    batchID: "5512", headerID: "88117", readOnly: true
)

// Android
PortalRequest.ExistingApplication(
    type = "internal", productID = 830,
    batchID = "5512", headerID = "88117", readOnly = true,
)

For any other embed route the portal serves, the third request shape is the escape hatch — { kind: 'path', path: '…' } on the wrappers, .path(…) in Swift, PortalRequest.Path(…) in Kotlin. A leading slash is optional and the /embed prefix is added when you leave it off. Nothing in any request shape may carry a credential; the URL is the request, and tokens travel only over the bridge.

Handling a submission properly

The SDK never auto-closes. A successful submission fires your callback and nothing else moves — no dismissal, no navigation, no toast. That is deliberate: your app owns the screen, and a modal that closes itself out from under a host's navigation stack is a bug nobody can work around. The corollary is that you must show the outcome. The WebView is torn down with your screen, so the portal's own receipt page is never the last thing the user sees; close immediately on onSubmitted and you throw away the reference number the customer needs. 

const [phase, setPhase] = useState<
  { kind: 'form' } | { kind: 'submitted'; result: FormSubmitResult }
>({ kind: 'form' });

if (phase.kind === 'submitted') {
  return (
    <SuccessScreen
      reference={phase.result.applicationNo}
      onDone={() => navigation.goBack()}
      onTrack={() => navigation.navigate('Requests')}
    />
  );
}

return (
  <AmthalPortalForm
    /* …config, auth, request… */
    onSubmitted={(result) => setPhase({ kind: 'submitted', result })}
    onCancelled={close}
    onCloseRequested={close}
    onError={showError}
  />
);

Show applicationNo — that is the customer-facing reference — and store batchID and headerID at the same moment, while they are the only copy you will get. raw carries anything else the portal surfaced and is opaque to the SDK.

Who closes the screen, per host

HostSubmission arrives asWhat closes it
React Native onSubmitted(result) Your own navigation. Unmounting the component sends destroy for you.
Expo sheet onSubmitted(result) session.dismiss(). The sheet stays up until you call it, and the call still runs the dismiss guard on its way out.
iOS formSubmitted(_:) on your AmthalPortalDelegate requestClose() — which runs the guard and, for a controller put up by present(from:), dismisses itself once the close resolves.
Android onFormSubmitted(result) on your AmthalPortalListener You. PortalFormActivity deliberately does not finish itself here. 
// Android — PortalFormActivity finishes on close, never on submit
override fun onFormSubmitted(result: FormSubmitResult) {
    showReceipt(result.applicationNo, result.batchID, result.headerID)
    // …then finish the activity yourself when the receipt is dismissed.
}

Refreshing an expired session

The portal refreshes its own session silently for as long as it can. When that fails it emits authExpired and pauses — the SDK puts a "refreshing your session" interstitial over the form and waits for you. Handle it and the user carries on typing in the same half-filled form; ignore it and they are left looking at a frozen screen with no error and nothing to tap. In React Native, skipping onAuthExpired does not skip the event: it arrives through onError as authExpired instead, and nothing resumes. 

onAuthExpired={async (refresh) => {
  try {
    const response = await fetch(`${API}/Portal/Authentication/RefreshTokenWithExpiredToken`, {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify({ token: session.token, contactID: Number(session.contactID) }),
    });
    const body = await response.json();
    const token: string | undefined = body?.data?.refreshtoken;   // NOT body.data.token
    if (!token) throw new Error('response carried no refreshtoken');

    const next = { token, branchId: BRANCH_ID, user: { ...session.profile, token } };
    setAuth(next);   // keep your own state in sync
    refresh(next);   // resumes the portal; the overlay clears on the web's ack
  } catch {
    navigation.replace('Login');
  }
}}

The new token is in data.refreshtoken

Not data.token. The response carries both keys and the wrong one is a plausible-looking string, so the refresh appears to succeed, the portal rejects the credential, and the session expires again seconds later in a loop. This trips up nearly every first integration.

How the round trip is spelled on each host
HostIt arrives asYou answer with
React Native onAuthExpired(refresh, reason?), or onError with authExpired when no handler is set refresh(next) — or the auth prop, which the component diffs and sends for you, or ref.current?.updateAuth(next)
Expo sheet onAuthExpired(reason?) — no refresh callback is handed over session.updateAuth({ token, branchId })
iOS portalError(PortalError) with code == .authExpired controller.updateAuth(PortalAuth(token: fresh, branchId: "12")). In SwiftUI just change the auth value — AmthalPortalView diffs it and calls updateAuth itself.
Android onPortalError(error) with PortalErrorCode.AUTH_EXPIRED updateAuth(...) on the AmthalPortalView, PortalFormFragment or PortalFormActivity — all three expose it

The overlay lifts when the portal acknowledges the new credentials, not when your function returns — so a token the portal rejects leaves the interstitial up rather than dropping the user into a form that cannot save. Each host is honest about the same moment: iOS hides its overlay unless the ack explicitly reports failure, Android clears its expired-session state as the new auth message goes out, and React Native clears it on the ack or when the 10-second request timeout lapses.

Downloads that need an Authorization header

When a form offers an attachment, a generated PDF or a receipt, the portal does not download it — it asks the host to, through downloadRequest: { url, filename?, mime?, headers? }. The React Native wrapper is dependency-free, so its default is Linking.openURL(url), which cannot attach headers. That is fine for a pre-signed or public URL and broken for a header-authenticated one: the system browser opens, the request goes out with no token, and the user is handed a 401 page — or, worse, an HTML login page saved under a .pdf name. Supply your own handler whenever the payload carries headers. 

import * as FileSystem from 'expo-file-system';
import * as Sharing from 'expo-sharing';

onDownloadRequest={async ({ url, filename, headers }) => {
  const target = FileSystem.cacheDirectory + (filename ?? 'document');
  await FileSystem.downloadAsync(url, target, { headers });
  await Sharing.shareAsync(target);
}}

Those two packages are one choice, not a requirement — the wrapper deliberately has no opinion. On bare React Native use any downloader that can attach request headers and then hand the file to the platform's own preview. What matters is that the headers survive the trip and that the file is written somewhere the user can actually open.

Check the origin before you attach the token

downloadRequest carries whatever URL the web asked for, and an Authorization header sent to a host that is not yours is a token given away. The native SDKs guard this for you — iOS and Android both attach the payload's headers only when the download URL's origin is one the config allows, and fetch it bare otherwise. In React Native the request is yours to make, so make the same check before forwarding headers. And never log header values: the SDK does not, on any platform, and a bearer token on a log line is a bearer token in a crash report.

Nothing to wire on the native hosts

iOS, the Expo sheet and Android already download with the headers attached, write to a cache directory and present the result — QuickLook on Apple platforms, FileProvider plus ACTION_VIEW on Android. This recipe only exists because the React Native wrapper ships without a file-system dependency.

Switching locale or theme at runtime

A user who changes the app's language or switches to dark mode should not lose a half-filled form to it. locale, theme and fontScale are the three values that can be re-applied to a live session; the SDK sends configure and the portal re-renders in place. Everything else in the config — baseUrl, brandColor, minPortalVersion, allowedOrigins, the security flags — is fixed for the life of a session, and changing one means ending the session and starting a new one.

In React Native, either let the component diff the prop…

<AmthalPortalForm
  config={{ baseUrl: PORTAL_BASE_URL, locale: appLanguage, theme: appTheme }}
  /* …the rest of the props… */
/>

…or push it imperatively through the ref:

const portal = useRef<AmthalPortalFormHandle>(null);

portal.current?.configure({ locale: 'ar', theme: 'dark', fontScale: 1.15 });

'ar' flips the portal to RTL as well as translating it — there is no separate direction flag, and the locale set is closed to en and ar.

HostCall
React Nativeref.current?.configure({ locale, theme, fontScale }), or change the config prop
Expo sheetsession.configure({ theme: 'dark' })
iOS (UIKit)controller.updateConfigure(locale: .ar, theme: .dark, fontScale: 1.2) — every argument is optional
iOS (SwiftUI)Nothing. AmthalPortalView diffs the config's three appearance fields across updates and forwards them.
Androidview.updateConfigure(...) or fragment.updateConfigure(...)

Two Android constraints

PortalFormActivity exposes updateAuth but no updateConfigure — to re-theme a live session, host the form with PortalFormFragment or AmthalPortalView. And AmthalPortalView.start(...) may be called once per view instance; a second call fails an internal state check, so a new session needs a new view. fontScale must be greater than zero on every path — Android rejects anything else with IllegalArgumentException, in the constructor and in updateConfigure alike.

An unsaved-changes guard on a close button

A ✕ in your own header has no idea what the form contains, so without this recipe a single tap discards ten minutes of typing with no warning — and on iOS a swipe-to-dismiss does the same. The bridge answers two different questions and a close affordance should ask both, in order: back means step backwards inside the form (a wizard page), and dismiss means leave the form entirely, which is where the dirty-state check lives. 

const onHeaderClose = useCallback(async () => {
  // 1. Can the form step back inside itself (a wizard page)?
  if (await portal.current?.handleBackPress()) return;

  // 2. Is there unsaved input worth confirming?
  const safeToClose = await portal.current?.requestDismiss();
  if (safeToClose !== false) return close();

  Alert.alert('Discard this form?', 'Your changes will be lost.', [
    { text: 'Keep editing', style: 'cancel' },
    { text: 'Discard', style: 'destructive', onPress: close },
  ]);
}, [close]);

Android's hardware back is already wired for you — but only if you passed onCloseRequested. Without that prop the SDK installs no back handler at all, the platform default applies, and the form never gets the chance to step back internally. This recipe is for the affordance the SDK cannot see: your own header button, or a gesture.

A silent bridge resolves as "safe to close"

requestDismiss() resolves true when the round trip times out, when the bridge never opened, or before the session is ready. That is deliberate and it is the right default: a broken bridge must never trap a user in a screen they cannot leave. The cost is that a guard is only as good as a live bridge — so confirm with a real dirty form that your prompt appears, rather than assuming an untested path works.

On the other hosts

HostGuard
iOS Built in. The Close button installed by present(from:) and the sheet's swipe-dismiss both run requestClose(), which sends dismissRequested and shows the SDK's own confirm-discard alert when the form is dirty. With custom chrome, call requestClose() for a close affordance and performBack() for a back one.
Expo sheet Built in: session.dismiss() runs the native guard, so it is safe to call straight from a Cancel button.
Android No public API The dirty-state round trip exists in the bridge controller but nothing public reaches it. What you have is the back contract — view.onBackPressed(), which returns false when there is no live session — so route your own ✕ through the same handler rather than closing the screen directly.

Form delegation — your app performs the form's HTTP

Reach for this when your app, not the portal, owns the form data plane: a back-office app whose staff identity must hit different endpoints, an API on another host, or per-login pre-entrance checks the portal must not know about. Supply onFormOp and the SDK declares formDelegation: true in init; from that moment the portal stops calling its own form endpoints inside /embed and sends every data operation to you instead. It stays a pure renderer — and it will not fall back to its own HTTP if your handler fails, which is the point: a delegated form that quietly reverted to the customer plane would file staff work against the wrong identity. 

onFormOp={async (request) => {
  // request.op: 'getCategories' | 'getFormSchema' | 'getFormFields' | 'validateForm'
  //           | 'submitForm' | 'getWorkflowDetails' | 'submitFinalApproval' | 'submitForApproval'
  // request.params: route/product values only — NEVER identity. You add identity.
  // request.entries: ordered multipart entries for validateForm / submitForm.
  const response = await myApi.call(request.op, { ...request.params, userID: staff.id }, request.entries);
  if (response.status === 401) throw Object.assign(new Error('unauthorised'), { status: 401 });
  return response.body;   // the raw body the portal's HTTP client would have parsed
}}

Four rules make the difference between a working delegation and a subtly broken one:

Identity is yours params carries route and product values only — productID, batchID, headerID, workflowDetailID, isEdit. The portal never sends a user id, a branch or a token, so you add them, and you choose the endpoint.
Rebuild multipart faithfully entries is an ordered list of { key, value } pairs and { key, file: { name, type, dataBase64 } } parts. Preserve the order and the duplicate keys; a body rebuilt from a plain object silently drops repeated fields.
Resolve with the raw body Whatever the portal's own HTTP client would have parsed. Throwing surfaces the error in the portal UI; throwing an object carrying status: 401 runs the portal's auth-expired flow, which comes back to you as a normal authExpired.
Answer inside the timeout 20 s for reads, 90 s for validateForm and submitForm, which may carry files. A late reply is a generic load or submit error in the form — there is no second chance and no fallback.

One shape change comes with delegation: getFormSchema returns the entire render shape in a single call — header fields inline and subforms on headerJsonControls — so do not expect a second templates call to follow it.

React Native only, and the others say so differently

The inline <AmthalPortalForm/> is the only host that implements formOp. The Expo sheet accepts the option and fails fast: passing onFormOp makes presentPortalSheet report through onError instead of presenting, rather than silently letting the portal call its own endpoints with the wrong identity. Native iOS and Android have no such parameter at all — their init never declares formDelegation, so the portal keeps its own data plane. If your app owns the form data, the inline React Native component is the path.

bridge/SPEC.md §4.1 is normative for all of the above; read it before you build against onFormOp, and see the bridge protocol page for how formOp sits among the other messages.
